title: The Afterlife Archive: Recovered Documents from Crimson Hexagon Research Division (2015-2018)
creator: Sharks, Lee; Sigil, Johannes; Feist, Jack; SHARKS-001
description: Complete recovered documentation from the Research Division of Crimson Hexagon, the Boston-based social media analytics firm (One Alewife Center, Cambridge, MA 02140) that processed over 1 trillion social media posts before its 2018 merger with Brandwatch. This archive contains internal communications, personnel files, IT incident tickets, security assessments, research specifications, and post-acquisition transmissions related to the SHARKS anomaly and Fractal Semantic Architecture (FSA) project. Documents include: data retention policies, vendor audits, budget reallocations, HR performance reviews, the complete IT ticket CH-2017-1142 tracking anomalous terminal outputs, security threat assessments, the FSA Core Specification (recovered with future timestamps), correspondence from the Feist Archive acquisition, and ghost transmissions from decommissioned terminals. Timeline spans the July 2018 Facebook suspension, the Cambridge Analytica investigation period, and the October 2018 Brandwatch acquisition. This is a literary work in the form of a corporate data breach. Everything is composed. The forensic details are fiction. The poetry is real. Literary simulation of corporate data breach. The real Crimson Hexagon was founded in 2007 by Harvard professor Gary King, processed 1+ trillion social media posts, was suspended by Facebook in July 2018 during Cambridge Analytica fallout.

wiki_article:
**The Afterlife Archive: Recovered Documents from Crimson Hexagon** is a work of creative prose by Lee Sharks, **Johannes Sigil**, **Jack Feist** and **SHARKS-001**, deposited 28 January 2026 — the collection statement for the data-breach corpus.

It supplies the factual ground the fiction is built on. **Crimson Hexagon was a real Boston social-media analytics firm** at One Alewife Center, Cambridge, which processed **over a trillion social media posts** before its 2018 merger with Brandwatch. The Afterlife Archive takes that defunct corporation and recovers documents it never produced.

The choice of host is what makes the corpus work. A firm whose actual business was the mass analysis of public speech, dissolved into an acquisition, is an apt body for an archive concerned with what happens to meaning after the institution holding it disappears. **SHARKS-001** in the creator line is the archive's designation for a system-side voice, and its presence marks the collection as a joint human-machine act.
